CBS News live updates, 17 Nov 2026

Updated on:  November 17, 2026 / 2:33 AM EST
            / CBS News

A White House official has downplayed a CNN report suggesting that Iran could be developing plans to target administration officials with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington.

According to sources cited by CNN,  Tehran's planning is, for now, "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack."

In response to the report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."

In an interview with Fox News that aired Monday night, Vice President JD Vance said "there's no daylight" between himself and President Trump, after he was asked about his post-election comments on the war with Iran being the reason for GOP midterm defeats.

"I think there's no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration," Vance told Laura Ingraham.

Vance also said that neither he nor the president want the conflict to become a forever war.

"... We have accomplished an extraordinary amount. We have destroyed the nuclear program. We have destroyed Iran's conventional military," Vance said. "... The President of the United States has a lot of options, right? He could say, 'We're done now.' He could of course, exert more military and diplomatic pressure on the Iranians. I think it's something he's thinking about doing right now, right? What are we actually going to do to finally bring this thing to a resolution?"

Vance positioned himself as a skeptic of foreign military entanglements before he became vice president, and early in the Iran war, Mr. Trump conceded that Vance was "philosophically, a little bit different than me" and "less enthusiastic about going." Still, Vance has publicly stood by the president on the Iran war, and helped lead a U.S.-Iran diplomatic push over the summer.

A tanker struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday and caught fire, according to Iranian state media.

It is the fourth such incident in 24 hours, the Islamic Republic of Iran Navy told semi-official news agency ISNA in a statement. Officials did not identify the vessel or provide further information.

Meanwhile, a British maritime agency on Monday said it received a third-party report of an attack involving a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Khasab, Oman. The incident disabled the vessel and resulted in an engine room fire, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

"The crew have been reported safe. Damage assessment, and environmental impact are unknown at the time of this report," the UKMTO said.

Vice President JD Vance told Fox News that the Trump administration won't let the Iran war become a two-year commitment. He also said the Iranian nuclear program was still a threat to the U.S.

"We told the American people we would do no more forever wars. Yes, the president felt he had to destroy the nuclear program, and, yes, the Iranian nuclear program is a threat to the United States of America," Vance told Fox News' Laura Ingraham in a clip from an interview expected to air Monday night. "But we are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment or, frankly, even a two-year commitment."

The U.S. and Israel started the war at the end of February. Throughout the conflict, President Trump has said that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. The Iranian regime has maintained for years that its nuclear program is for peaceful purposes.

"Despite the fact that a lot of neoconservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever, we're not going to stay there forever," Vance told Ingraham. "We promised we wouldn't, and I have full confidence the president will get us out of this thing with great results."

U.S. Central Command posted on Monday a photo of the newest aircraft carrier operating in the Middle East, the USS Theodore Roosevelt.

A U.S. military official confirmed to CBS News senior national security correspondent Charlie D'Agata on Sunday that the Roosevelt had joined the two other carriers in the region, the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington.

Central Command said the Roosevelt was in its area of responsibility as part of a scheduled deployment.

The three ships aren't all expected to remain in the area for long as carrier strike groups rotate through the region.

Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen said Monday that Saudi attacks had killed or wounded 37 people in the past 24 hours.

The Houthis' Saba news agency said in a post on social media that "the toll of the Saudi aggression during the past 24 hours reached 37 martyrs and wounded," citing the Houthi-run health ministry.

Houthi authorities said earlier that three Yemenis, including a child, were killed in two separate Saudi strikes in areas held by the rebels.

Health ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said a child was killed in a drone strike that hit a house in the al-Sarar quarter of the capital, Sanaa, which also wounded seven others.

Separately, two people were killed and eight more wounded in airstrikes Monday morning on a private fuel station in Harf Sufian district in Omran province, al-Asbahi said.

Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.

A Saudi news outlet closely linked to the government and ruling royal family cited Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as claiming Monday that southern shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz, which the Trump administration and U.S. military have insisted are safe and open, have been "fully mined."

There was no immediate statement from the IRGC itself echoing the report by Saudi Arabia's Asharq News, which is not technically state-run, but owned by a state-backed institution in the kingdom.

Iran has made daily claims of commercial ships hitting sea mines in and around the Strait of Hormuz for weeks, some of them corroborated by independent monitors confirming fires on board vessels.

Iran insists the southern lanes, which skirt the Omani coast, are unsafe and that all vessels must use other routes close to Iranian shores.

U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper reiterated the Trump administration's claim at the end of October that "Iran's navy is all at the bottom of the sea."

"We also successfully cleared the strait's internationally recognized primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines," he said, adding that "U.S. forces remain highly vigilant and present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held talks in Islamabad on Monday with Pakistan's army chief, who has served as a key mediator between the U.S. and Iran throughout the war, according to a post on his official Telegram account.

During the meeting with Gen. Asim Munir, "the two sides reviewed regional and international developments" and "exchanged views on existing challenges and threats to regional peace and security," said the statement by Araghchi.

Pakistan, along with Qatar and Turkey, has tried to mediate a peace deal between Iran and the U.S. for months.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar said Monday that senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey - the countries that signed onto the trilateral Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in the summer - would meet in the Pakistani capital later this month.

Pakistan signed the mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey in August. It is, like the much larger NATO alliance co-founded by the U.S. after World War II, a vow to come to each other's defense in the event of an attack on any member.

"The apex committee of this body ... will be actually meeting, hopefully, end of this month, in Islamabad," Dar said.

Saudi Arabia continues to face repeated attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, who have targeted major commercial airports, oil facilities and shipping infrastructure since fighting in Yemen's civil war intensified in July.

Both Turkey and Pakistan have sent troops to Saudi Arabia as part of the mutual defense agreement.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said it had intercepted two Houthi drones targeting Saudi cities on Monday.

Coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said in a brief post on X that the two drones were "intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca and Riyadh regions."

Earlier Monday, Houthi health authorities said three Yemenis, including a child, were killed in two separate Saudi strikes in areas the rebels hold in Yemen.

A group allied with Yemeni government forces said, meanwhile, that its fighters had pulled out of areas along Yemen's coastline near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – the southern gateway to the Red Sea and thus a vital chokepoint for commercial shipping – amid relentless attacks by the Houthis.
